# Consensus, tool dropout, and permissivity of RNA-editing callers

**Dataset:** `examples/Morales_et_al_small` (6 samples: WT and ADAR1KO, 3 clones each; 3 aligners: STAR, BWA, HISAT2)
**Generated by:** `examples/Morales_et_al_small/results/tool_comparison/correlation/consensus_analysis/consensus_analysis.py`
**Figures:** [`figures/consensus_analysis/`](figures/consensus_analysis/)

> **MARINE / SPRINT note (2026 refactor).** The PNGs in
> `figures/consensus_analysis/` predate the addition of MARINE to this analysis and
> the MARINE `coverage ≥ 5` post-hoc filter; their pixels are unchanged, but the
> MARINE rows added to the tables below come from the current matrices and should
> be treated as the up-to-date figures. **SPRINT is retained in this analysis doc**
> (it is a de-novo caller worth characterizing); only the automated
> `results/tool_comparison/` matrices exclude SPRINT.

## Inputs

All analysis is computed from the three site × `tool.aligner.sample` matrices in
`results/tool_comparison/compare_all_tools/` (5000 union sites, all aligners/samples pooled):

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `edit_coverage_matrix.tsv` | read depth at each called site |
| `edit_fraction_matrix.tsv` | editing fraction |
| `tool_score_matrix.tsv`    | per-tool score / QUAL / probability |

**Critical caveat — the matrices are heterogeneously populated.** Each tool only fills
the field(s) it natively reports, so a naïve cross-tool average is meaningless
(it produced an impossible "edit fraction" of 2.0 in a first pass). The corrected
conventions used throughout:

- **Depth** is taken only from `{bcftools, jacusa2_call1, reditools}` (the tools that report a true read depth ≥5).
- **Edit fraction** is taken from **REDItools** (the canonical 0–1 reporter; median ≈0.04–0.14).
- **Scores** are kept on their own per-tool axes (bcftools = QUAL, jacusa2 = test statistic, redinet/red_ml = class probability).
- **MARINE** reports `count` and `coverage` (no native edit fraction); its fraction is computed as `count/coverage`, and its rows are gated at `coverage ≥ params.marine.min_coverage` (default 5) — so MARINE's call volume here is already coverage-filtered, comparable to the depth floor applied to the other quantitative callers.
- `reditools3` is an **exact duplicate** of `reditools` and is excluded from tool counting.

A site is "called" by a tool if it is nonzero in *any* of the three matrices for that tool's columns.

## 1. Consensus vs non-consensus sites

![consensus](figures/consensus_analysis/consensus_vs_private.png)

Agreement groups (collapsing the reditools/reditools3 duplicate): **private = 1 tool, shared = 2, consensus ≥ 3.**

| group | sites |
|---|---|
| private (1 tool) | 3244 |
| shared (2 tools) | 315 |
| consensus (≥3 tools) | 1441 |

**Headline findings:**

- **Non-consensus sites are essentially JACUSA2 noise.** 99.2 % of private sites (3219/3244) are called by JACUSA2 and nobody else; the rest are 15 bcftools-only, 7 sprint-only, 3 red_ml-only.
- **Private sites are unquantified.** Only **0.5 %** of private sites have any real read-depth value, versus **100 %** of consensus sites. Non-consensus calls are statistical calls that no quantitative caller corroborates.
- Among REDItools-quantified sites, both **edit fraction** and **depth** rise steeply with agreement (consensus depth median ≈556×). REDItools never appears as a lone caller, so it always corroborates ≥1 other tool.
- **MARINE strengthens the consensus tier:** as an independent de-novo caller (~1,195 sites) it overlaps heavily with the REDItools/JACUSA2 sets — 864 of its sites are also called by JACUSA2 and 645 by REDItools. Only **317 (27 %)** are MARINE-private; **781 (65 %)** are corroborated by ≥2 other tools, so MARINE contributes mostly to the shared/consensus groups, not the JACUSA2-dominated private tier.
- JACUSA2's own test statistic is only modestly higher for consensus than private calls (0.087 vs 0.066, Mann-Whitney p = 2.9 × 10⁻⁷) — the agreement gap is driven by *lack of quantitative support*, not by the JACUSA2 score alone.

Per-comparison medians and Mann-Whitney p-values: [`consensus_stats.tsv`](figures/consensus_analysis/consensus_stats.tsv).

## 2. Why SPRINT and the ML tools (redinet / red_ml) miss sites

![dropout](figures/consensus_analysis/sprint_ml_dropout.png)

The two ML tools reach the REDItools candidate set for **completely different reasons** — a point cross-checked against `pipelines/Morales_et_al/rules/tools.smk`:

| tool | input (rule) | constraint | REDItools overlap |
|---|---|---|---|
| **redinet** | REDItools `outTable.gz` (`rule redinet`, `tools.smk:527`) | **code-enforced** — it classifies rows of a REDItools table | **100 % (structural)** |
| **red_ml** | rmdup **BAM** (`rule red_ml`, `tools.smk:242`) | **none** — `red_ML.pl` derives candidates itself, then filters by dbSNP / simpleRepeat / Alu / p-value | **81 % (emergent)** |

> ⚠️ **Correction:** an earlier draft claimed red_ml was "structurally a subset of REDItools candidates." That is wrong. red_ml runs independently on the BAM; 3/16 of its calls fall *outside* the REDItools set. Only **redinet** is code-locked to REDItools candidates.

**Why they call so few sites:**

- Both are **high-precision edit-fraction filters**, not depth filters. REDItools candidates that an ML tool also flags have far higher REDItools edit fraction (median 0.98 vs 0.03, p = 6 × 10⁻¹⁰) and are kept even at *lower* depth (59 vs 535).
- Of the 11 candidates redinet scores, it labels **8 as SNP** (`ed_proba ≈ 0`) and endorses only 3 as editing; red_ml's 16 calls all have probability > 0.5 (0.52–0.97).
- They structurally cannot recover JACUSA2-only or bcftools-only sites (redinet never sees them; red_ml's filters reject them).

**SPRINT** is an independent caller: it runs its own hyper-editing / SNV-cluster detection from the BAM with **no shared candidate list**. In this small dataset it makes 14 low-support calls (median 1 supporting read), half of them private, and is essentially **orthogonal** to the candidate-based tools — it shares only 7 sites with REDItools and 7 with JACUSA2.

**MARINE** is also an **independent de-novo caller**, not a candidate-based classifier: it scans the BAM per chromosome (`marine_by_chrom`, `tools.smk`), then its output is restricted to the configured `strand_conversion` (A>G) and gated at `coverage ≥ params.marine.min_coverage` (default 5). Unlike the high-precision ML filters, MARINE is comparatively **permissive** — in this dataset it reaches ~1,195 sites, second only to the JACUSA2/REDItools group — so it corroborates many REDItools sites while also contributing its own. Because it derives candidates itself, it can call sites the candidate-locked tools (redinet) structurally cannot.

## 3. Permissivity / stringency of all tools

![permissivity](figures/consensus_analysis/tool_permissivity.png)

Permissivity is proxied (no ground-truth set exists) by **call volume** plus the tendency to emit **low-confidence / uncorroborated** calls.

**Sites called (descending):**

| tool | sites called | category |
|---|---|---|
| **jacusa2** | **4848** | de-novo editing caller |
| jacusa2_call1 | 1756 | de-novo editing caller |
| reditools | 1513 | de-novo editing caller |
| marine | ~1195 | de-novo editing caller |
| bcftools | 109 | DNA / germline caller |
| red_ml | 16 | ML classifier |
| **sprint** | **14** | de-novo editing caller |
| redinet | 11 | ML classifier |

> MARINE's count (~1,195) is taken from the current matrices and **predates the
> `coverage ≥ 5` filter** added in the 2026 refactor; the post-filter count will be
> somewhat lower but stays in the high-hundreds-to-thousands range — it does not
> change MARINE's rank or any claim below.

### ✅ Claim 1 — JACUSA2 calls the most sites and is the most permissive: **VERIFIED**

- `argmax(call volume) = jacusa2` (4848 sites, 2.8× the next caller).
- Only **34 %** of JACUSA2 calls are seen by any other tool — it emits the most unique/uncorroborated sites.
- JACUSA2 (call-1) accepts variants with **~100× lower edit fraction** than REDItools (median EF 0.0018 vs 0.040), i.e. it is far less stringent on edit-fraction.
- It is run in the most permissive configuration (pooled `all_samples`, call-2 mode).

### ✅ Claim 2 — SPRINT is the most stringent: **VERIFIED (with a caveat)**

- Among the genome-scanning **de-novo editing callers** (`jacusa2, jacusa2_call1, reditools, marine, sprint`), `argmin(call volume) = sprint` (14 sites).
- **MARINE does not change this:** it is the *most permissive* of the de-novo callers after the JACUSA2/REDItools group (~1,195 sites), nearly two orders of magnitude above SPRINT — it sits at the opposite end of the stringency axis from SPRINT.
- **Caveat:** `redinet` (11) and `red_ml` (16) produce comparably few or fewer sites, but they are **downstream classifiers/filters**, not de-novo callers — they cannot call anything beyond a pre-filtered candidate pool. Among tools that scan the alignments de novo, **SPRINT is the most stringent.**

### Reproduce

```bash
module load python3essential
python3 examples/Morales_et_al_small/results/tool_comparison/correlation/consensus_analysis/consensus_analysis.py
```
